name: Slow-Roasted Beef Tenderloin
headnote: J. Kenji Lopez-Alt argues that tenderloin's problem is its leanness: with no marbling to insulate it, it cooks fast and develops a wide band of overcooked grey meat before the centre is ready, and overcooked lean meat goes cottony. His answer is the reverse sear, roasting the tied roast at 225F until the centre is just under the serving temperature so the meat is nearly uniform edge to edge, then browning it at the very end. He also pretreats: salting heavily and resting the roast uncovered in the fridge overnight dissolves myosin so the meat shrinks and expels less liquid, and dries the surface into a pellicle that browns fast, which is the one advantage this method holds over sous vide's wet exterior. The finish is brown butter with shallot and thyme poured over the roast, then about two minutes under a broiler with a turn every 30 seconds.
comment_digest: The dominant correction, repeated by nearly every reviewer, is that the stated two-to-three-hour roast is far too long: three- to four-pound roasts routinely hit 120 to 125F in 60 to 100 minutes, and one reviewer complains the wide range is useless for timing a dinner party. Several describe holding the roast successfully, pulling it early and wrapping it in foil or a towel-lined cooler for an hour or two, then returning it briefly to a 200 to 225F oven to recover temperature before searing. Use a leave-in probe and insert it straight rather than diagonally; one cook found a slanted probe reading ten degrees low. On the finish, roughly 30 seconds per turn for about two minutes total is the consensus, and going longer starts a grey rim; one suggests leaving the ends tied so the roast does not flop under the broiler. A minority found the overnight salting much too salty.
flags: Helpfulness counts exist but top out at 1, so ranking by votes is weak. Several near-duplicate reviews are posted by the same accounts (one cook posted essentially the same review three times, another posted 'too salty' twice), which slightly inflates those signals. Comments truncated at 'Read More'.
